excerpt: New (American) gal in town, San Francisco vocalist Noa Levy joins the trio of UK 2023 Parliamentary Award winning pianist Paul Edis with eminent reedman Alan Barnes added to three of the 10 tracks. All titles are associated with Bill Evans. The human voice (Levy's) is the central feature of this (not entirely successful) experiment. Barford and Barnes are more successful in this self-imposed task than Levy. This is an ambitious album with Edis, Barnes, King and Barford in sterling form throughout. Levy is inconsistent but also shows promise.

Two-CD issue of a live recording of his trio (Dave Holland, bass and Eliot Zigmund, drums) performing at the Kuumbwa Jazz Centre in Santa Cruz, California on 17 May 1987. Zev Feldman's diligent research located previously unknown recordings. These were early days for the diminutive and severely handicapped Petrucciani, but his daring, virtuosity and musical intelligence were already evident. Every track on this newly unearthed buried treasure confirms these judgments. Standards include Stella By Starlight, Autumn Leaves, My Funny Valentine.

Brian Morton's sleeve-note questions whether Ray Charles was a jazz singer, an R&B singer or a pop singer. He was clearly all of those but several of the albums he recorded during the 50s and early 60s really established his jazz credentials. The first six titles here were arranged by Quincy Jones. With his inimitable approach as a song stylist he makes these selections all his own especially the soulful Georgia On My Mind. 20th Century Masterworks LP.

The titles on this vinyl reissue come from the quintet's first studio date. Sweet Clifford is a contrafact of Sweet Georgia Brown, taken at a blistering tempo of 80 bpm. The easy-paced Stompin' At The Savoy, with its call and response routine, is a perfect vehicle for the group and Brown's use of sub-tone in his lower register is very impressive. The Clifford Brown-Max Roach quintet, along with Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers, really defined the hard-bop era.

album: The Big Soul Of John Lee Hooker
excerpt: Part of a combined review of three reissues: Ray Charles: The Genius Of Ray Charles, Clifford Brown-Max Roach Quintet: Brown and Roach Inc., and John Lee Hooker: The Big Soul Of John Lee Hooker. Gordon Jack reviewing.

Vocalist Siril Malmedal Hauge once more joins with pianist Kjetil Mulelid on this release. The Norwegian pair have worked together, and it shows, as an old friendship shows to a stranger. Filled with originals and a few carefully chosen covers. Hauge's vocals, when a cappella, can seem a bit chilly. Mulelid's playing can be a bit dry from time to time but there are some excellent moments where his glissandos shine. The softer, moody tone they take throughout seems very Scandinavian.

Vienna-born but London-based saxophonist Guido Spannocchi rethinks the chamber music of his childhood through a clever jazzy lens. The pieces on here have a contemporary feel. Songs like DKT exhibit vibraphone to add a glimmering effect. It moves the atmosphere to a 1950s or 60s era, similar to Henry Mancini's material. Other tracks, such as Kivu, match a klezmer chamber-sound with jazz saxophone. Spannocchi has a decidedly European perspective with Yiddish influence.
Part of a combined review with Siril Malmedal Hauge & Kjetil Mulelid and Guido Spannocchi. Konstantin N. Rega reviewing.

In a musical landscape where virtually every new title promoted as 'jazz' would be unrecognizable to the musicians who actually created it, circa 1895, in New Orleans, it's refreshing to encounter a new release that not only acknowledges those pioneers but also respects and honours them, and one in particular, George Lewis. Leon Nock reviewing.

album: For Ev'ry Man There's A Woman
excerpt: Part of a combined review with Alyn Shipton's New Orleans Friends: The Oxford Concert. Leon Nock reviewing.

During the 1970s French singer and entertainer Sacha Distel performed a number of times at the London Palladium and on British TV, and on these visits he would drop into Collets Jazz Shop. This album from 1956 was issued originally on Atlantic. Matthew Wright reviewing.
Part of a combined review with John Lewis & Sacha Distel: Afternoon In Paris and Melissa Aldana: Filin. Matthew Wright reviewing.
Part of a combined review with John Lewis & Sacha Distel: Afternoon In Paris and McCoy Tyner: The Seeker. Matthew Wright reviewing. Melissa Aldana at the Newport festival in 2022.

Veteran French bassist Henri Texier is calling on past compositions of his to be applied as balm to brows fevered by the current anxiety-provoking atmosphere. His quintet, with guest drummer Manu Katché on three of the nine tracks, performs the music he found comforting when he wrote it. Octogenarian Texier has a style that has remained personal and consistent throughout his career. Nigel Jarrett reviewing.
Part of a combined review with Henri Texier: Healing Songs, Mark Wade Trio and Joe Lovano. Nigel Jarrett reviewing.
Part of a combined review with Henri Texier: Healing Songs and Anat Cohen Quartetinho. Nigel Jarrett reviewing.

album: New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival 2026
excerpt: The New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival, now in its 55th year, increasingly looks like a major rock and pop festival, with a series of niche festivals running alongside the headline acts. The conundrum with the ongoing moniker of Jazz Fest is that to sustain a profitable festival, the vast majority of festival-goers attend for the non-jazz acts. Live review from Jazz Journal.
